title: Ὁδοιπόροι καὶ φρύγανα
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 258. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὁδοιπόροι κατά τινα αἰγιαλὸν ὁδεύοντες ἦλθον ἐπί τινα σκοπιάν.
sentences.tr: Hodoiporoi kata tina aigialon hodeuontes ēlthon epi tina skopian.
sentences.l: Travellers journeying along a certain shore came to a certain lookout point.
sentences.n: σκοπιά is a height one looks out from — a headland or watch-place. The whole fable turns on their seeing from far off.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖθεν θεασάμενοι φρύγανα πόρρωθεν ἐπιπλέοντα, ναῦν εἶναι μεγάλην ᾠήθησαν.
sentences.tr: Kakeithen theasamenoi phrygana porrōthen epipleonta, naun einai megalēn ōiēthēsan.
sentences.l: And from there, having seen brushwood floating at a distance, they supposed it to be a large ship.
sentences.n: Κἀκεῖθεν is καὶ ἐκεῖθεν run together by crasis. φρύγανα are dry sticks, the brushwood gathered for kindling. οἴομαι takes the accusative and infinitive: 'they supposed it to be a ship'.

sentences.t: Διὸ δὴ προσέμενον, ὡς μελλούσης αὐτῆς προσορμίζεσθαι.
sentences.tr: Dio dē prosemenon, hōs mellousēs autēs prosormizesthai.
sentences.l: Therefore indeed they waited on, on the ground that she was about to put in to shore.
sentences.i: So they waited, expecting the ship to come in to land.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute, μελλούσης αὐτῆς, with ὡς marking the reason as the travellers' own supposition rather than the narrator's report. αὐτῆς is feminine because ναῦς is.

sentences.t: Ἐπεὶ δὲ ὑπὸ ἀνέμου φερόμενα τὰ φρύγανα ἐγγυτέρω ἐγένετο, οὐκέτι ναῦν, ἀλλὰ πλοῖον ἐδόκουν βλέπειν.
sentences.tr: Epei de hypo anemou pheromena ta phrygana engyterō egeneto, ouketi naun, alla ploion edokoun blepein.
sentences.l: But when the brushwood, being carried by the wind, came nearer, they thought they were looking no longer at a ship, but at a boat.
sentences.n: ναῦς is the great sea-going ship, πλοῖον any smaller craft; the thing keeps shrinking as they get a better look at it. ὑπό with the genitive gives the agent, here the wind.

sentences.t: Ἐξενεχθέντα δὲ αὐτὰ φρύγανα ὄντα ἰδόντες, πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἔφασαν ὡς ἄρα μάτην ἡμεῖς τὸ μηδὲν ὂν προσεδεχόμεθα.
sentences.tr: Exenechthenta de auta phrygana onta idontes, pros allēlous ephasan hōs ara matēn hēmeis to mēden on prosedechometha.
sentences.l: But having seen them, once cast ashore, being brushwood, they said to one another that — so it turned out — in vain were we waiting for the thing that is nothing.
sentences.i: But when they saw them washed ashore, and saw that they were brushwood, they said to one another that they had been waiting, to no purpose, for a thing that was nothing at all.
sentences.n: The report opens with ὡς, 'that', and then slides into the speakers' own words — ἡμεῖς … προσεδεχόμεθα, 'we were waiting' — a common Greek shift from indirect to direct. ἄρα marks the discovery, 'so that is how it was'. τὸ μηδὲν ὄν is an articular participle, 'the thing that is nothing'.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἔνιοι ἐξ ἀπροόπτου δοκοῦντες φοβεροὶ εἶναι, ὅταν εἰς πεῖραν ἔλθωσιν, οὐδενὸς εὑρίσκονται ἄξιοι.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti tōn anthrōpōn enioi ex aprooptou dokountes phoberoi einai, hotan eis peiran elthōsin, oudenos heuriskontai axioi.
sentences.l: The fable shows that some among men, seeming at first sight to be formidable, whenever they come to the test, are found worthy of nothing.
sentences.n: ἐξ ἀπροόπτου is 'unexpectedly', literally 'out of what has not been foreseen'; what is meant is the sudden first look, taken before a thing has been made out — the travellers' own mistake. εἰς πεῖραν ἐλθεῖν is to come to the trial of a thing, and ἄξιος takes the genitive of what one is worth.
